title: Urda crash audio, mortgage rates and car compensation
summary:
New audio reveals the orders given before the deadly train collision near Urda. We examine the mortgage outlook, housing uncertainty and pension changes, plus a compensation ruling for car buyers and a dispute over fibre costs.

Enjoying Spain Daily? Support us: https://buymeacoffee.com/spanified

segments.speaker: Dima
segments.body: I'd like a mortgage breather. Are we getting one?

segments.speaker: Inna
segments.body: Euribor is heading towards three point two percent. Down from three point three. nice

segments.speaker: Dima
segments.body: Good. So are variable-rate mortgages safe, or about to go up again?

segments.speaker: Inna
segments.body: The central bank meets today. We'll come back to that after the news.

segments.speaker: Dima
segments.body: Good morning. It's Thursday, the twenty-ninth of October, and this is Spain Daily, from Spanified dot com!

segments.speaker: Inna
segments.body: I'm Inna, here with Dima. Later, a fight over your internet bill: one side says eight cents, the other says one euro fifty. And a better deal for car buyers. First, the deadly train collision near Urda.

segments.speaker: Dima
segments.body: Audio reveals an official at Adif, the rail infrastructure manager, authorised an AVE to proceed at 'normal speed' before yesterday's collision near Urda, in Toledo province. El Mundo reports at least sixty-eight people died and dozens were injured. The AVE hit a stopped Iryo train on the Madrid–Andalusia high-speed line.

segments.speaker: Inna
segments.body: The Government blames human error after a safety-system failure. Most parties suspended election events.

segments.speaker: Dima
segments.body: Inna, what exactly did the audio show about the orders?

segments.speaker: Inna
segments.body: The AVE driver asked for confirmation, and the official repeated it: normal speed. Nobody recommended slowing down to proceed with caution. The Iryo was already stopped ahead.

segments.speaker: Dima
segments.body: Was the backup system still supervising the trains' speed and distance continuously?

segments.speaker: Inna
segments.body: No. After the main safety system failed that morning, trains switched to a backup without continuous speed supervision.

segments.speaker: Dima
segments.body: And this is the second deadly crash on this line this year. In January, forty-six people died at Adamuz.

segments.speaker: Inna
segments.body: Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez promised to investigate to the end. The general election is on the twenty-ninth of November.

segments.speaker: Dima
segments.body: Now, back to my question. Will the central bank raise rates today?

segments.speaker: Inna
segments.body: Veinte Minutos reports Euribor is heading towards three point two percent for October, down from September. It's the main benchmark for variable-rate mortgages. Markets expect the European Central Bank to hold rates today. Investment manager Pimco forecasts an increase in December.

segments.speaker: Dima
segments.body: A small drop. I'll take it. But a December hike could push it higher again.

segments.speaker: Inna
segments.body: And inflation is three point eight percent, a three-year high. I wouldn't count on this relief lasting.

segments.speaker: Dima
segments.body: Housing has its own uncertainty. Expansión reports one housing decree approved on October sixth is already in force. It extends certain rental contracts by two years and restricts purchases by companies and large holders. Investors say uncertainty has stalled funding, developments and rental contracts. Investment firm Azora has nearly a billion euros available that could go elsewhere.

segments.speaker: Inna
segments.body: Huh. For a tenant, that's protection now. But then why are the funds waiting?

segments.speaker: Dima
segments.body: Parliamentary approval is pending, and investors are waiting for the election and the next government's housing policies.

segments.speaker: Inna
segments.body: So the two-year extension already applies. right But Azora's money could go to other markets in the meantime.

segments.speaker: Dima
segments.body: Inna, who gets a widow's pension today, and who would be added?

segments.speaker: Inna
segments.body: Couples with children who never married or registered their partnership would qualify under the Government-approved reform, El País reports. The average widow's pension is just under a thousand euros monthly, compared with about sixteen hundred for retirement. Widow's pension numbers have been falling as marriages decline and more women receive retirement pensions.

segments.speaker: Dima
segments.body: Most widow's pensions go to women, so this matters. But is it fair that a pension depends on a wedding paper?

segments.speaker: Inna
segments.body: The children are the condition here. Couples without children aren't covered by this reform. Fair or not, that's the line.

segments.speaker: Dima
segments.body: Employment protection is changing too. El País reports the Supreme Court voided thirty-one terminations at Avanade Spain, including sixteen voluntary departures. The court counted restructuring-linked exits towards the collective dismissal threshold. Workers must be reinstated with back pay. Anyone who received severance must return it.

segments.speaker: Inna
segments.body: Wait, why count people who agreed to leave? That sounds different from being dismissed.

segments.speaker: Dima
segments.body: The company's own documents linked those departures to its restructuring. The court said the exits couldn't be considered separately.

segments.speaker: Inna
segments.body: That's harsh for people who took severance. But the company never ran the consultation with worker representatives.

segments.speaker: Dima
segments.body: A better result for some car buyers: the Supreme Court raised compensation against Stellantis España, El Diario reports. A group of Citroën buyers affected by the manufacturers' price-fixing cartel will receive five percent of the purchase price. That's up from two percent. The October twenty-second ruling strengthens other buyers' claims.

segments.speaker: Inna
segments.body: Oh, that's a welcome increase. What does the higher percentage mean for someone considering a claim?

segments.speaker: Dima
segments.body: A stronger basis for seeking compensation for the overcharge. oh nice The court considered the earlier award too small.

segments.speaker: Inna
segments.body: And with more cartel rulings coming, law firms are competing harder for claimants.

segments.speaker: Dima
segments.body: El País reports Spain's six largest banks must hold about four billion euros more in top-quality capital from January first next year. Much of the rise follows the Banco de España raising a buffer against economic risks. Those banks already hold a combined surplus of roughly a hundred and ninety-three billion euros above minimum requirements.

segments.speaker: Inna
segments.body: Four billion euros more. Does that mean tougher loans for us?

segments.speaker: Dima
segments.body: Not necessarily, they have big cushions already. Still, the banks are lobbying in Brussels against rising capital demands.

segments.speaker: Inna
segments.body: For cash payments, Heraldo reports the EU's adopted business-payment cap starts on July tenth next year, at ten thousand euros. Spain's stricter thousand-euro limit stays when a business or self-employed professional is involved. Non-resident individuals acting privately have a ten-thousand-euro exception. Private-to-private payments fall outside the EU cap.

segments.speaker: Dima
segments.body: Really, no change to everyday business payments here? That EU headline sounds much bigger than the effect in Spain.

segments.speaker: Inna
segments.body: Spain keeps its lower limit. The EU rule mainly brings countries allowing larger cash payments under a shared ceiling.

segments.speaker: Dima
segments.body: Until now Brussels set no cap at all. Each country made its own rules, and the aim is to fight money laundering.

segments.speaker: Inna
segments.body: Finally, the internet-cost dispute. El País reports Telefónica wants voluntary commitments to replace regulated access to ducts carrying fibre cables. Rivals say costs would rise by one euro fifty per customer monthly. They're asking Spain's competition regulator to reject the proposal.

segments.speaker: Dima
segments.body: Telefónica puts the rise at up to eight cents per line. The regulator's final decision is pending.

segments.speaker: Inna
segments.body: Eight cents against one euro fifty. Who do we believe?

segments.speaker: Dima
segments.body: Rivals point to a steep cumulative rise over five years. Telefónica points to a small final step per line. The regulator hasn't decided yet.

segments.speaker: Inna
segments.body: Coming up: the central bank decision today, eurozone growth figures tomorrow, and the general election on November twenty-ninth.
